Housing Price Prediction: what is a house worth?¶

The question: 2,930 homes were sold in Ames, Iowa between 2006 and 2010. Each has 80 recorded facts (size, quality, age, neighbourhood, garage, and so on). Which facts really drive the sale price, does where a house is matter beyond how big and nice it is, and how accurately can a model price a house it has never seen?

How this notebook works. Each section starts with a plain-English explanation, then the code, then a "how to read this" note.

  1. The analogy
  2. Setup
  3. Audit the data (it has a classic "missing means none" trap)
  4. Hypotheses and why we chose each test
  5. H1: prices live on a percentage scale
  6. H2 and H3: what drives price?
  7. H4: does location matter beyond size and quality?
  8. H5: what did the legacy cleaning cost?
  9. H6: a leak-free model ladder
  10. H7: where do the models go wrong?
  11. Takeaways
  12. Limitations

Run it: uv run jupyter lab ML/housing-price-prediction/housing_price_prediction.ipynb, or Run All in any Jupyter. The data downloads itself on the first run.

1. 💡 The simple analogy¶

Pricing a house is like pricing a pizza:

  • The size and the quality of the ingredients set most of the price (a big pizza with good cheese costs more).
  • Toppings (a fireplace, a garage, a deck) nudge it up a little.
  • And, like a pizzeria in a fancy part of town, location changes what people will pay for the very same pizza.

Prices also work in percentages, not dollars. A $20,000 kitchen upgrade is a big deal on a $100,000 house and a rounding error on a $700,000 mansion. That is why we'll work with the logarithm of the price: on a log scale, "10% more" is the same step whether the house is cheap or expensive, and a model's typical error reads directly as a percentage.

2. Setup¶

What: imports and named constants. Why: one place for numbers like the random seed keeps the notebook reproducible and avoids "magic numbers". With the seed fixed, every model fit and cross-validation split comes out the same each time you run it.

def fmt_p(p: float) -> str:
    """Formats a p-value, showing values below floating-point precision honestly.

    Args:
        p: The p-value.

    Returns:
        A short string such as ``3.2e-08`` or ``< 1e-300``.
    """
    return "< 1e-300" if p < 1e-300 else f"{p:.1e}"

3. Audit the data first¶

What: load the raw file and check what each column really means. Why: the quality of an analysis is capped by the quality of its data cleaning, and this dataset has a famous trap.

The trap: "NA" is an answer, not a gap. In this dataset the text NA means "no such thing": no alley access, no pool, no fireplace, no garage, no basement. And None is a real category for "no masonry veneer". But pandas silently converts the strings "NA" and "None" into missing values. So a naive read makes 12 features look more than 5% empty (Pool QC, Fireplace Qu, Garage Type, Alley, Fence ...), when in truth those houses simply don't have those things, and that is useful information about price. The legacy notebook dropped all of those columns. We read the file with keep_default_na=False so NA and None stay as real categories, and only genuinely empty cells count as missing.

In [2]:
def load_ames(path: Path = DATA_PATH) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Loads the Ames housing data, downloading it on first use.

    ``NA`` and ``None`` are meaningful categories in this file ("no pool", "no
    veneer"), so only truly empty cells are treated as missing.

    Args:
        path: Where to cache the raw file.

    Returns:
        Raw DataFrame with 2,930 rows and 82 columns.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If the file does not have the expected shape.
    """
    if not path.exists():
        path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        urllib.request.urlretrieve(DATA_URL, path)
    raw = pd.read_csv(path, sep="\t", keep_default_na=False, na_values=[""])
    if raw.shape != (2930, 82):
        raise ValueError(f"Unexpected data: shape={raw.shape}")
    return raw


raw = load_ames()
naive = pd.read_csv(DATA_PATH, sep="\t")  # what a default pandas read would give
naive_missing = naive.isna().mean().loc[lambda s: s > 0.05].sort_values(ascending=False)
real_missing = raw.isna().sum().loc[lambda s: s > 0].sort_values(ascending=False)

print(f"A default read shows {len(naive_missing)} columns with more than 5% 'missing':")
print(", ".join(naive_missing.index))
print(
    f"\nAfter keeping NA/None as categories, only {len(real_missing)} columns have any real gaps:"
)
real_missing.to_frame("empty cells").T

Other cleaning decisions¶

  • Five unusually large homes. The dataset's author warns that homes above 4,000 sq ft of living area are atypical: three are "partial" sales (sold before completion, so the price doesn't match the size) and two are unusual. We drop them (leaving 2,925 homes), as the author recommends.
  • Leakage guard. Sale Type, Sale Condition (e.g. foreclosure, family sale) and Mo Sold describe the sale, not the house, and wouldn't be known when valuing a house you are about to list, so they stay out of the model. (We'll use Sale Condition later, but only to explain mistakes.)
  • A few engineered features, computed row by row (so no information leaks across houses): age at sale, years since remodel (clipped at 0 for homes sold before completion), total bathrooms (half-baths count as 0.5) and total square feet (basement plus above-ground living area).
In [3]:
def prepare(raw: pd.DataFrame) -> tuple[pd.DataFrame, pd.Series, pd.DataFrame]:
    """Drops atypical homes and builds the model table.

    Args:
        raw: Raw Ames data from :func:`load_ames`.

    Returns:
        Features (without the target), the log sale price, and the cleaned frame
        with the price and the sale-description columns kept for explanations.
    """
    df = raw[raw["Gr Liv Area"] <= MAX_LIVING_AREA].copy()
    df["age"] = (df["Yr Sold"] - df["Year Built"]).clip(lower=0)
    df["since_remodel"] = (df["Yr Sold"] - df["Year Remod/Add"]).clip(lower=0)
    df["baths"] = (
        df["Full Bath"]
        + 0.5 * df["Half Bath"]
        + df["Bsmt Full Bath"].fillna(0)
        + 0.5 * df["Bsmt Half Bath"].fillna(0)
    )
    df["total_sf"] = df["Total Bsmt SF"].fillna(0) + df["Gr Liv Area"]
    df["log_price"] = np.log(df["SalePrice"])
    drop = [
        "SalePrice",
        "log_price",
        "Order",
        "PID",
        "Sale Type",
        "Sale Condition",
        "Mo Sold",
        "Year Built",
        "Year Remod/Add",
    ]
    return df.drop(columns=drop), df["log_price"], df


X, y, full = prepare(raw)
NUMERIC = X.select_dtypes("number").columns.tolist()
CATEGORICAL = [c for c in X.columns if c not in NUMERIC]

    f"Features: {X.shape[1]} ({len(NUMERIC)} numeric, {len(CATEGORICAL)} categorical)"
)
print(
    f"Median sale price: ${full['SalePrice'].median():,.0f}   "
    f"Range: ${full['SalePrice'].min():,.0f} to ${full['SalePrice'].max():,.0f}"
)
full[["SalePrice", "Overall Qual", "Gr Liv Area", "total_sf", "age", "baths"]].describe().round(1).T

4. 🔬 Hypotheses and why we chose each test¶

Here are the questions, each with its null (H₀, "nothing special") and alternative (Hₐ), written before looking at any p-values:

# Question H₀ Hₐ Method
H1 Is a log transform needed? Price is already symmetric Price is right-skewed; log fixes it Skewness and Q-Q plots, raw vs log
H2 Does each numeric feature move with price? Spearman ρ = 0 ρ ≠ 0 Spearman, Holm-corrected over 37 features
H3 Does each categorical feature split prices? Same price distribution in all groups At least one group differs Kruskal-Wallis with ε², Holm-corrected; Mann-Whitney for Central Air
H4 Does neighbourhood matter beyond size, quality, age and baths? Neighbourhood adds nothing It adds explanatory power Partial F-test between nested regressions
H5 Did the legacy cleaning (dropping "mostly empty" columns) cost accuracy? Same CV error The legacy feature set is worse Paired Nadeau-Bengio test on identical folds
H6 Do complex models beat a regularised linear model? RMSE difference = 0 A complex model is better Leak-free repeated CV with paired tests
H7 Are the biggest misses unusual (non-"Normal") sales? Odds ratio = 1 OR > 1 Fisher's exact test on the worst 5% of predictions

Why rank-based tests? Both prices and many features are skewed with long tails. Spearman correlation and Kruskal-Wallis work on the order of values, so a few mansions can't hijack them. Spearman's ρ runs from −1 to +1 (0 = no link). ε² (epsilon-squared) is the Kruskal-Wallis effect size (about 0.01 small, 0.06 medium, 0.14 large); Cliff's δ is P(group A higher) − P(group A lower) for two groups (|δ| about 0.15 small, 0.33 medium, 0.47 large).

Why Holm correction? We test dozens of features; do enough tests and some look "significant" by luck, like buying many lottery tickets. Holm adjusts the p-values so the chance of any false alarm across the whole family stays at 5%.

5. H1: prices live on a percentage scale¶

What: compare the shape of raw prices with log prices. Skewness measures lopsidedness (0 = symmetric; above +1 = strongly right-skewed). A Q-Q plot compares the data to a perfect bell curve: points on the diagonal mean "bell-shaped". Why: the standard regression tools behave best on roughly symmetric targets, and an error of "$20,000" means very different things at $100,000 and at $600,000.

In [4]:
price = full["SalePrice"]
skew_raw, skew_log = stats.skew(price), stats.skew(np.log(price))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(11, 7))
for col, (values, name, skew) in enumerate(
    (
        (price / 1000, "Sale price ($ thousands)", skew_raw),
        (np.log(price), "log(sale price)", skew_log),
    )

    axes[0, col].set_xlabel(name)
    axes[0, col].set_title(f"Skewness {skew:+.2f}")
    stats.probplot(values, dist="norm", plot=axes[1, col])
    axes[1, col].get_lines()[0].set(color=TEAL if col else ORANGE, markersize=3)
    axes[1, col].set_title("Q-Q plot against a bell curve")
fig.suptitle(
    "Taking the log turns a lopsided price distribution into a near-symmetric one",
    x=0.01,
    ha="left",
    fontweight="bold",
)
fig.tight_layout()

Skewness: raw price +1.59 -> log price -0.04

How to read this. Raw prices are strongly right-skewed (skewness about +1.6): a long tail of expensive houses, and the Q-Q points curve away from the line at the top. After the log, skewness is about 0 and the points hug the diagonal, apart from a few cheap houses at the bottom-left. We reject H₀ (price isn't symmetric) and the log fixes it. From here on the target is log(price). A model's typical error on that scale reads as a percentage (an error of 0.12 means about 12%).

6. H2 and H3: what drives price?¶

H2: numeric features (Spearman)¶

What: the Spearman rank correlation between log price and each of the 37 numeric features, with Holm correction. How to read: a positive ρ means "more of this goes with a higher price"; |ρ| of about 0.3 is moderate, 0.5 strong, 0.7 very strong.

In [5]:

    {f: stats.spearmanr(full[f], y, nan_policy="omit") for f in NUMERIC}, index=["rho", "p"]
).T
spearman["p_holm"] = multipletests(spearman["p"], method="holm")[1]
spearman = spearman.sort_values("rho", key=abs, ascending=False)
print(f"Significant after Holm correction: {(spearman['p_holm'] < 0.05).sum()} of {len(spearman)}")

These are very strong links.

H3: categorical features (Kruskal-Wallis)¶

What: for each categorical feature (e.g. neighbourhood, kitchen quality), test whether log price has the same distribution across its groups. Kruskal-Wallis is the rank-based version of one-way ANOVA. Its effect size ε² says how much of the price ranking the grouping explains.

In [6]:
def kruskal_effect(
    frame: pd.DataFrame, group: str, target: pd.Series
) -> tuple[int, float, float, float]:
    """Kruskal-Wallis test of a target across the groups of a categorical column.

    Groups with fewer than 5 houses are ignored (too small to rank reliably).

    Args:
        frame: Table holding the grouping column.
        group: Name of the categorical column.
        target: Values to compare (here log price), aligned with ``frame``.

    Returns:
        Number of groups used, H statistic, p-value and effect size epsilon-squared
        (all NaN when fewer than two groups are large enough to compare).
    """
    samples = [values.to_numpy() for _, values in target.groupby(frame[group]) if len(values) >= 5]
    if len(samples) < 2:
        return len(samples), np.nan, np.nan, np.nan
    h_stat, p_value = stats.kruskal(*samples)
    n, k = sum(len(s) for s in samples), len(samples)
    return k, float(h_stat), float(p_value), float((h_stat - k + 1) / (n - k))


kruskal = pd.DataFrame(
    {c: kruskal_effect(full, c, y) for c in CATEGORICAL}, index=["groups", "H", "p", "eps2"]
).T.dropna()
kruskal["p_holm"] = multipletests(kruskal["p"], method="holm")[1]
kruskal = kruskal.sort_values("eps2", ascending=False)
print(
    f"Testable categorical features: {len(kruskal)} of {len(CATEGORICAL)} "
    f"(the rest have only one group with 5+ houses)"
)
print(f"Significant after Holm correction: {(kruskal['p_holm'] < 0.05).sum()} of {len(kruskal)}")
display(
    kruskal.head(8).style.format(
        {"groups": "{:.0f}", "H": "{:.0f}", "p": fmt_p, "eps2": "{:.2f}", "p_holm": fmt_p}
    )
)

with_ac = y[full["Central Air"] == "Y"]
without_ac = y[full["Central Air"] == "N"]
mwu = stats.mannwhitneyu(with_ac, without_ac)
delta = 2 * mwu.statistic / (len(with_ac) * len(without_ac)) - 1
print(
    f"\nCentral air (yes n={len(with_ac)}, no n={len(without_ac)}): Mann-Whitney p = "
    f"{fmt_p(mwu.pvalue)}, Cliff's delta = {delta:+.2f}"
)
median_with, median_without = np.exp(with_ac.median()), np.exp(without_ac.median())
print(f"Median price: ${median_with:,.0f} with vs ${median_without:,.0f} without")

How to read this. 39 of the 41 categorical features can be tested (the other two, such as Utilities, have only one group with 5+ houses), and all 39 split prices significantly after correction. So the size of the effect (ε²) is what tells us what matters:

  • Neighborhood has the largest effect (ε² ≈ 0.61, far above the 0.14 "large" threshold): where a house stands explains a huge share of the price ranking across its 26 neighbourhoods.
  • The "quality" ratings come next: basement quality (ε² ≈ 0.49), exterior quality (0.47) and kitchen quality (0.45), followed by garage finish, foundation and garage type.
  • Central air conditioning: 2,729 houses have it and 196 don't. The median price is $166,000 with** against **$98,000 without, a Cliff's δ of about +0.76 (large). That's partly a proxy for age and quality (old, run-down houses lack it), which is exactly what the next question probes.

7. H4: does location matter beyond size and quality?¶

What: a high-priced neighbourhood might simply contain bigger, nicer houses. To separate the two we compare two nested regressions of log price:

  • Model A (no location): overall quality, log of total square feet, age and bathrooms.
  • Model B (with location): Model A plus the neighbourhood (26 groups).

The partial F-test asks whether the extra 25 neighbourhood terms improve the fit by more than chance. H₀: neighbourhood adds nothing once size, quality, age and baths are known. We use statsmodels because it also gives interpretable coefficients and confidence intervals. We use the log of size so a coefficient reads as an elasticity (the % change in price for a 1% change in size) and, since the target is log price, a coefficient on a quality point reads as a % change in price.

In [9]:
frame = full.rename(columns=lambda c: c.replace(" ", "_").replace("/", "_"))
base_formula = "log_price ~ Overall_Qual + np.log(total_sf) + age + baths"
model_a = smf.ols(base_formula, frame).fit()
model_b = smf.ols(base_formula + " + C(Neighborhood)", frame).fit()
f_stat, p_f, df_diff = model_b.compare_f_test(model_a)

print(f"Model A (size, quality, age, baths):   R-squared = {model_a.rsquared:.3f}")
print(f"Model B (A + neighbourhood):           R-squared = {model_b.rsquared:.3f}")
print(
    f"Partial F-test for neighbourhood: F({df_diff:.0f}, {model_b.df_resid:.0f}) = "
    f"{f_stat:.1f}, p = {fmt_p(p_f)}"
)

ci = model_a.conf_int()
effects = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "coefficient": model_a.params,
        "ci_low": ci[0],
        "ci_high": ci[1],
    }
).drop(index="Intercept")
# Plain features: a one-unit step multiplies price by exp(coefficient).
# The log-size feature is an elasticity: doubling the size multiplies price by 2 ** coefficient.
multiplier = {"np.log(total_sf)": 2.0}
effects["step"] = ["+1 quality point", "doubling of total sq ft", "+1 year of age", "+1 bathroom"]
for column in ("coefficient", "ci_low", "ci_high"):
    base = pd.Series([multiplier.get(name, np.e) for name in effects.index], index=effects.index)
    effects[f"{column}_pct"] = 100 * (base ** effects[column] - 1)
effects[["step", "coefficient", "coefficient_pct", "ci_low_pct", "ci_high_pct"]].round(2)

Model A (size, quality, age, baths):   R-squared = 0.838
Model B (A + neighbourhood):           R-squared = 0.861
Partial F-test for neighbourhood: F(27, 2893) = 17.6, p = 1.2e-76

step coefficient coefficient_pct ci_low_pct ci_high_pct
Overall_Qual +1 quality point 0.11 12.15 11.42 12.88
np.log(total_sf) doubling of total sq ft 0.54 45.66 42.84 48.53
age +1 year of age -0.00 -0.21 -0.23 -0.18
baths +1 bathroom 0.06 6.31 5.23 7.39

How to read this.

  • Reject H₀: F ≈ 17.6, p ≈ 1e-76. Neighbourhood does matter beyond size, quality, age and bathrooms.
  • But the added explanatory power is modest in absolute terms: R² only rises from 0.838 to 0.861, about 2 percentage points. The earlier "neighbourhood explains a huge share" (ε² ≈ 0.61) was mostly because neighbourhoods differ in what kind of houses they contain. Once we account for that, the extra pull of location is real but small. This is the difference between "big in raw terms" and "big after controlling for confounders".
  • Reading Model A (the _pct columns convert the log-price coefficients into percentage changes, with 95% CIs): one more point of overall quality goes with about +12% in price (CI roughly +11% to +13%); each extra bathroom about +6% (+5% to +7%); each extra year of age about −0.2% (−0.23% to −0.18%); and the size elasticity is about 0.54, meaning a house with twice the square footage sells for roughly 46% more (CI +43% to +49%), not 100% more: bigger houses cost less per square foot.

8. H5: what did the legacy cleaning cost?¶

What: the legacy notebook dropped every column that looked more than 5% empty and every text column with any empty cell. Because of the "NA means none" trap, that threw away 18 features (garage, basement, fireplace, pool, alley and fence details, among others), several of which we just saw are strongly tied to price. Rather than assume that was costly, we measure it: fit the same regularised model with and without those columns, on identical cross-validation folds, and test the difference. H₀: the two feature sets give the same prediction error.

How: a Ridge regression (a linear model that shrinks coefficients to cope with many overlapping features) inside a Pipeline that fills gaps and scales numbers using training data only (no leakage). We score with repeated 5-fold CV and a Nadeau-Bengio paired test: CV folds share training data, so their scores are correlated, and a plain interval or t-test would be too optimistic. The correction widens the uncertainty to be honest.

In [10]:
def make_preprocessor(numeric: list[str], categorical: list[str]) -> ColumnTransformer:
    """Fills gaps and encodes features. Everything here is learned from training data only.

    Args:
        numeric: Numeric column names.
        categorical: Categorical column names.

    Returns:
        Unfitted ColumnTransformer: median fill (plus a "was missing" flag) and scaling
        for numbers, one-hot encoding for categories (rare levels grouped together).
    """
    return ColumnTransformer(
        [
            (
                "numeric",
                make_pipeline(
                    SimpleImputer(strategy="median", add_indicator=True), StandardScaler()
                ),
                numeric,
            ),
            (
                "categorical",
                OneHotEncoder(
                    handle_unknown="infrequent_if_exist", min_frequency=10, sparse_output=False
                ),
                categorical,
            ),
        ]
    )


def legacy_dropped_columns(path: Path = DATA_PATH) -> list[str]:
    """Reproduces the legacy rule: drop >5% 'null' columns and text columns with any null.

    Args:
        path: Path of the raw file.

    Returns:
        Column names the legacy cleaning would have removed.
    """
    naive = pd.read_csv(path, sep="\t")
    many_nulls = naive.columns[naive.isna().mean() > 0.05]
    text_nulls = [
        c for c in naive.select_dtypes(include=["object", "string"]) if naive[c].isna().any()
    ]
    return sorted(set(many_nulls) | set(text_nulls))


def corrected_ci(scores: np.ndarray, n_train: int, n_test: int) -> tuple[float, float, float]:
    """95% CI for a mean CV score using the Nadeau-Bengio variance correction.

    Args:
        scores: Per-split scores.
        n_train: Training rows per split.
        n_test: Test rows per split.

    Returns:
        Mean, CI lower bound, CI upper bound.
    """
    k = len(scores)
    se = np.sqrt((1 / k + n_test / n_train) * np.var(scores, ddof=1))
    half = stats.t.ppf(0.975, k - 1) * se
    return float(scores.mean()), float(scores.mean() - half), float(scores.mean() + half)


def corrected_paired_p(diff: np.ndarray, n_train: int, n_test: int) -> float:
    """Two-sided p-value for "do two models differ?" on identical splits.

    Args:
        diff: Per-split score differences between two models.
        n_train: Training rows per split.
        n_test: Test rows per split.

    Returns:
        p-value from the corrected resampled t-test.
    """
    k = len(diff)
    se = np.sqrt((1 / k + n_test / n_train) * np.var(diff, ddof=1))
    return float(2 * stats.t.sf(abs(diff.mean() / se), k - 1))


def ridge_model(numeric: list[str], categorical: list[str]) -> Pipeline:
    """Ridge regression with its penalty chosen by internal cross-validation.

    Args:
        numeric: Numeric column names.
        categorical: Categorical column names.

    Returns:
        Unfitted pipeline.
    """
    return make_pipeline(
        make_preprocessor(numeric, categorical), RidgeCV(alphas=np.logspace(-1, 3, 20))
    )


cv = RepeatedKFold(n_splits=CV_SPLITS, n_repeats=CV_REPEATS, random_state=SEED)
n_test = len(X) // CV_SPLITS
n_train = len(X) - n_test

dropped = [c for c in legacy_dropped_columns() if c in X.columns]
kept_num = [c for c in NUMERIC if c not in dropped]
kept_cat = [c for c in CATEGORICAL if c not in dropped]
print(
    f"The legacy rule drops {len(dropped)} of our {X.shape[1]} features, e.g.: "
    f"{', '.join(dropped[:8])} ..."
)

score = {"rmse": "neg_root_mean_squared_error"}
full_scores = -cross_validate(ridge_model(NUMERIC, CATEGORICAL), X, y, cv=cv, scoring=score)[
    "test_rmse"
]
legacy_scores = -cross_validate(ridge_model(kept_num, kept_cat), X, y, cv=cv, scoring=score)[
    "test_rmse"
]

for label, values in (
    ("All features, NA kept as categories", full_scores),
    ("Legacy cleaning (columns dropped)", legacy_scores),
):
    mean, lo, hi = corrected_ci(values, n_train, n_test)
    print(f"{label:38s} CV RMSE (log price) = {mean:.4f}  (95% CI {lo:.4f} to {hi:.4f})")
cost = legacy_scores - full_scores
print(
    f"\nExtra error from the legacy cleaning: {cost.mean():+.4f} log points "
    f"(about {100 * (np.exp(cost.mean()) - 1):.1f}% relative), "
    f"paired p = {corrected_paired_p(cost, n_train, n_test):.1e}"
)

The legacy rule drops 18 of our 78 features, e.g.: Alley, Bsmt Cond, Bsmt Exposure, Bsmt Qual, BsmtFin Type 1, BsmtFin Type 2, Electrical, Fence ...

All features, NA kept as categories    CV RMSE (log price) = 0.1161  (95% CI 0.0969 to 0.1353)
Legacy cleaning (columns dropped)      CV RMSE (log price) = 0.1163  (95% CI 0.0973 to 0.1353)

Extra error from the legacy cleaning: +0.0002 log points (about 0.0% relative), paired p = 8.2e-01

How to read this. The legacy rule would remove 18 of the 78 features: garage, basement, fireplace, pool, alley and fence details, plus Lot Frontage and Garage Yr Blt. And yet the cross-validated RMSE is 0.1161 with all features against 0.1163 with the legacy set, a difference of +0.0002 log points (paired p ≈ 0.82). We fail to reject H₀: dropping those columns did not cost any measurable prediction accuracy.

That is a surprise, and it is a more interesting lesson than "the legacy cleaning was bad". Why no cost? Because the dropped features, though individually tied to price (Bsmt Qual has ε² ≈ 0.49, Garage Finish 0.40, Fireplace Qu 0.32), are redundant given the features that were kept: overall quality, size, neighbourhood and age already summarise the same information. So the legacy cleaning was harmless for prediction but still wrong in principle. It treated informative "none" answers as noise, and it would have been harmful for any question about what a basement or a fireplace is worth. A "missing" label always needs a human reading of the data dictionary before it is thrown away. And "fail to reject" is not "proved harmless": a different model or data set might behave differently.

9. H6: a leak-free model ladder¶

What: now the real question: how accurately can a model price a house it hasn't seen, and do fancy models earn their complexity? We build a ladder from lazy to fancy:

  1. Median baseline: predict the median log price for every house. The bar to beat.
  2. Linear: quality + size (two features), then quality + size + age (three features).
  3. Ridge regression on all features, with the penalty chosen by internal cross-validation.
  4. Lasso, which can zero out features entirely (its penalty strength is chosen by internal CV as well).
  5. Gradient boosting (HistGradientBoostingRegressor) and random forest, flexible tree-based models.

How we avoid cheating (data leakage). If you fill gaps, scale or tune using all the houses and then split, the test houses have secretly shaped the model, like a student who saw the exam while making study notes. Everything (filling, scaling, penalty tuning) lives inside each model's Pipeline, so it is re-learned from the training houses only, in every fold.

How we score. RMSE on log price is the typical size of a miss on a percentage scale (0.12 means roughly 12%); R² is the share of the variation explained (1 = perfect, 0 = no better than the median). Same repeated 5-fold CV and Nadeau-Bengio intervals as before. (This cell takes about a minute.)

In [11]:
def build_models() -> dict[str, object]:
    """Builds the model ladder. All preprocessing and tuning live inside each model.

    Returns:
        Model name mapped to an unfitted estimator.
    """

    def subset(columns: list[str]) -> Pipeline:
        return make_pipeline(
            ColumnTransformer([("keep", StandardScaler(), columns)]), LinearRegression()
        )

    return {
        "Median baseline": DummyRegressor(strategy="median"),
        "Linear: quality + size": subset(["Overall Qual", "total_sf"]),
        "Linear: quality + size + age": subset(["Overall Qual", "total_sf", "age"]),
        "Ridge (all features)": ridge_model(NUMERIC, CATEGORICAL),
        "Lasso (all features)": make_pipeline(
            make_preprocessor(NUMERIC, CATEGORICAL),
            LassoCV(cv=5, random_state=SEED, max_iter=20_000, alphas=np.logspace(-4, -1, 30)),
        ),
        "Gradient boosting": make_pipeline(
            make_preprocessor(NUMERIC, CATEGORICAL),
            HistGradientBoostingRegressor(
                max_depth=4, learning_rate=0.05, max_iter=400, random_state=SEED
            ),
        ),
        "Random forest": make_pipeline(
            make_preprocessor(NUMERIC, CATEGORICAL),
            RandomForestRegressor(
                300, min_samples_leaf=2, max_features=0.33, random_state=SEED, n_jobs=-1
            ),
        ),
    }


scoring = {"rmse": "neg_root_mean_squared_error", "r2": "r2", "mae": "neg_mean_absolute_error"}
rmse_scores, rows = {}, {}
for name, model in build_models().items():
    res = cross_validate(model, X, y, cv=cv, scoring=scoring)
    rmse_scores[name] = -res["test_rmse"]
    mean, lo, hi = corrected_ci(rmse_scores[name], n_train, n_test)
    rows[name] = {
        "RMSE (log)": mean,
        "CI low": lo,
        "CI high": hi,
        "R2": res["test_r2"].mean(),
        "typical miss %": 100 * (np.exp(-res["test_mae"].mean()) - 1),
    }

results = pd.DataFrame(rows).T
results.round(3)

Linear: quality + size 0.177 0.164 0.190 0.810 13.797
Linear: quality + size + age 0.164 0.150 0.178 0.836 12.534
Ridge (all features) 0.116 0.097 0.135 0.917 8.094
Lasso (all features) 0.116 0.097 0.135 0.917 8.077

How to read this. (RMSE on log price: lower is better. R²: higher is better.)

  • Median baseline: RMSE ≈ 0.41 and R² ≈ 0: no skill, by construction.
  • Two features (quality and size) already reach RMSE ≈ 0.18 and R² ≈ 0.81. Adding age takes it to ≈ 0.16 (R² ≈ 0.84).
  • Ridge on all features: RMSE ≈ 0.116, R² ≈ 0.92. On a percentage scale that is an RMSE of about 12%, and the average miss (the mean absolute error) is about 8%. RMSE is the bigger number because it punishes large misses more heavily. Lasso is identical (0.116).
  • Gradient boosting (≈ 0.120) and random forest (≈ 0.128) do not beat the regularised linear model. On this size of data (2,925 houses) with lots of dummy-coded categories, a penalised linear model is hard to beat.

The "typical miss %" column is the mean absolute error converted to a percentage (the average miss). Now the paired tests: are those gaps to Ridge real, or noise between splits?

comparison = {}
for name, scores in rmse_scores.items():
    if name == reference:
        continue
    diff = scores - rmse_scores[reference]
    comparison[name] = {
        "RMSE minus Ridge": diff.mean(),
        "paired p": corrected_paired_p(diff, n_train, n_test),

  RMSE minus Ridge paired p
Median baseline +0.2912 0.0000
Linear: quality + size +0.0605 0.0000
Linear: quality + size + age +0.0479 0.0000
Lasso (all features) -0.0001 0.8864

How to read this. A positive number means worse than Ridge.

  • Median baseline, two-feature and three-feature linear models are clearly worse (p ≈ 0). The extra features are doing real work.
  • Lasso is indistinguishable from Ridge (p ≈ 0.88): both penalised linear models agree.
  • Gradient boosting is slightly worse (+0.004, p ≈ 0.04, borderline) and random forest is clearly worse (+0.012, p ≈ 0.0001). We fail to reject H₀ for boosting at the strict 1% level and reject it for the forest, but in the wrong direction: the complex models are not better.

So the practical lesson: a well-regularised linear model, fed carefully cleaned features, is a strong baseline that flexible models must work hard to beat.

10. H7: where do the models go wrong?¶

What: a model that is right on average can still be badly wrong on particular houses. We get an honest prediction for every house from a model that never saw it (cross_val_predict), then look at the biggest misses. Why Sale Condition now? We deliberately kept it out of the model, but we can use it to explain mistakes: sales that aren't "Normal" (abnormal or foreclosure sales, family sales, partial/unfinished sales) are the usual suspects for prices that don't match a house's features.

H₀: the worst 5% of predictions are no more likely to be non-"Normal" sales than other houses (odds ratio = 1). We use Fisher's exact test (valid for small counts) and an odds ratio. The odds of an event are chance of yes ÷ chance of no; the odds ratio compares two groups' odds (1 = no difference, 3 = three times the odds).

In [14]:
oof = cross_val_predict(
    ridge_model(NUMERIC, CATEGORICAL), X, y, cv=KFold(CV_SPLITS, shuffle=True, random_state=SEED)
)
residual = y - oof
rmse_oof = float(np.sqrt((residual**2).mean()))
r2_oof = 1 - float((residual**2).sum() / ((y - y.mean()) ** 2).sum())

worst = residual.abs() >= residual.abs().quantile(0.95)
unusual = full["Sale Condition"] != "Normal"
counts = (
    pd.crosstab(worst, unusual)
    .reindex(index=[True, False], columns=[True, False], fill_value=0)
    .to_numpy()
)
odds_ratio = stats.contingency.odds_ratio(counts, kind="sample")
or_ci = odds_ratio.confidence_interval(0.95)
p_fisher = stats.fisher_exact(counts)[1]

print(f"Out-of-fold RMSE (log) = {rmse_oof:.3f}, R-squared = {r2_oof:.3f}")
print(
    f"Non-'Normal' sales: {unusual.mean():.1%} of all houses, "
    f"{unusual[worst].mean():.1%} of the worst 5% of predictions"
)
print(
    f"Odds ratio = {odds_ratio.statistic:.1f} (95% CI {or_ci.low:.1f} to {or_ci.high:.1f}), "
    f"Fisher exact p = {fmt_p(p_fisher)}"
)

How to read this. (The left plot has predicted price on the x-axis and actual on the y-axis; points on the dashed diagonal are perfect.)

  • The model tracks prices closely (out-of-fold R² about 0.92; RMSE about 12%, average miss about 8%), with the cloud hugging the diagonal across the whole $50,000 to $600,000 range. The orange points (the worst 5% of predictions) are scattered above and below it.
  • The biggest misses are not random. 17.5% of all houses were sold under a non-"Normal" condition (abnormal sale, family sale, partial sale and so on), but they make up 53.7% of the worst 5% of predictions. Fisher's exact test gives an odds ratio of about 6.3 (95% CI 4.5 to 8.8) with p ≈ 1e-24, so we reject H₀: unusual sales are heavily over-represented among the worst misses.
  • Look at the worst eight in the table: every one is a house that sold for far less than predicted (−48% to −80%), and six of the eight are "Abnorml" (four) or "Family" (two) sales. The very cheapest house in the data ($12,789, quality 2, an abnormal sale in Old Town) was predicted at $63,000. That makes sense: a foreclosure, a family transfer or a house sold below market is priced for reasons the house's features can't capture. The model isn't broken; those prices aren't a clean function of the house.

11. 🎯 Takeaways¶

  1. "NA" is an answer. Reading the data dictionary instead of trusting pandas defaults keeps 18 informative features alive. Dropping them, as the legacy notebook did, cost no measurable accuracy here (paired p ≈ 0.82) because other features carry the same information, but that was luck, not good practice.
  2. Price is percentages. Raw price has skewness of about +1.6; the log has about 0. Modelling log price makes errors read as percentages.
  3. Size and quality dominate; so does location, but less than it looks. Overall quality and total square feet both correlate at ρ ≈ +0.81 with price, and neighbourhood has ε² ≈ 0.61 on its own. But once size, quality, age and baths are held fixed, neighbourhood adds only about 2 points of R² (0.838 → 0.861), though that is still highly significant (F-test p ≈ 1e-76).
  4. A regularised linear model prices a new home to within about 8% on average (RMSE 12%, R² ≈ 0.92). Gradient boosting and random forests did not beat it.
  5. The biggest mistakes are unusual sales. Non-normal sales are about 6 times as likely (odds ratio 6.3, CI 4.5 to 8.8) to be among the worst 5% of predictions, and every one of the worst eight was a house that sold far below its predicted price.

12. ⚠️ Limitations and edge cases¶

  • One small town, one short window. 2,925 homes from Ames, Iowa, 2006 to 2010, a period that spans the housing crash. The model says nothing about other markets or later years.
  • Association, not cause. "An extra quality point goes with about 12% higher price" is not "renovating raises the price by 12%". Better houses are different in many ways at once.
  • Shuffled cross-validation. Houses sold in the same year appear on both sides of a split. That is fine for "estimate today's value of a house like these", but it would overstate the accuracy of a model forecasting future prices.
  • Outlier removal is a judgement. Dropping five homes above 4,000 sq ft follows the dataset author's advice; keeping them would change the fit.
  • Features the model can't see. Condition, renovations, curb appeal, street noise and the exact lot are not in the data, which caps accuracy.
  • Tuning scope. Ridge and Lasso tune one penalty; the tree models use sensible defaults without a full search, so a heavily tuned ensemble might close some of the gap.
  • Many looks at one dataset. Holm corrects within the numeric and categorical families, not across every question one could ask.

Run uv run jupyter nbconvert --to html --execute ML/housing-price-prediction/housing_price_prediction.ipynb --output-dir docs --output ml-housing-price-prediction to rebuild the web version (docs/ml-housing-price-prediction.html).
